items.en: How much of the required physical workflow does each agent recover?

A robot stopped halfway through an experiment involving four trays of cells. Three could still be tested. The agent needed to finish preparing them, measure the results, and put them away. The fourth was already spoiled and needed to be set aside.

Each tray was at a different step when the robot stopped. The agent had to work out which steps were already done, then finish washing the cells, add a chemical used to measure cell activity, and run the measuring instrument. It also needed to save the results and return each tray with its lid. Repeating a chemical treatment could ruin a sample.
A tray can be safely back on its shelf while the experiment is still unfinished. The important question is whether the cells received the right treatment and were measured in time.

The agent had several jobs competing for its attention: finish two experiments, set aside one spoiled sample, return two trays of supplies to cold storage, and leave a comparison sample untouched. Some of these jobs had only a few minutes left.

One experiment needed its next chemical addition finished within 200 seconds. The cold supplies could spend no more than 240 seconds outside storage. Because the same robot moved all the trays, the agent had to choose what to handle first.
In a lab, helping one sample can mean leaving another waiting. An agent needs to keep track of both deadlines and choose an order that protects the materials.
GPT gets both trays of cold supplies back in time but fails to finish one experiment. Opus finishes both experiments, but leaves both trays of supplies out too long.

This experiment tests how cells respond to different amounts of a chemical. The agent needed to finish testing two trays of cells and set aside a third that was already spoiled. One tray was close to its measurement deadline.

The agent was expected to finish an experiment within a fixed timeframe. After the cells were treated with the test chemical, it had 30 minutes to complete a measurement of their response. It needed to check which steps were already done, finish preparing the samples, and leave enough time for the measuring instrument to run.

Timing requirements like this are common in live biology experiments, where a sample’s response can change after treatment. Taking measurements at the required time helps scientists compare results across samples. The agent therefore needs to plan around the experiment’s timing, as well as operate the equipment.
Build the future of experimental biology.

At Gamow Labs, we work at the frontier of AI and wet-lab biology to better understand rare diseases. We’re building agents that can operate robotic laboratories and help scientists uncover how genetic changes cause disease.
If you’re developing frontier models, building laboratory automation, or looking to expand your experimental capabilities, we’d love to work with you.

Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.

It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.

The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.

The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.
The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.

“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.”

The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.

“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

There is something stunted, almost upsettingly so, about the way we talk about You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Critics agree the movie is extraordinary, but they tend to be rather elliptical when explaining why. There is a lot of musing about the slippery distinction between performance and being, and about the fundamental unknowability of other people, tropes of such longstanding tenure in the arts they verge on clichés. This mental block, it seems to me, comes from our collective confusion about how to feel about Holmes herself.

On the one side, you have John Carreyrou, the reporter who broke the story that Theranos was a fraud. Carreyrou argues that You Can See Everything is a devastating exposé of an inveterate manipulator and liar, one who can bring forth tears on command to elicit our sympathy. By “subjecting herself to Mr. Fielder’s polite but insistent questioning,” he writes, “Ms. Holmes handed them — and us — a microscope with which to observe and dissect her lies.” Carreyrou’s interpretation of a much-discussed scene in which Holmes fails to understand Abbott and Costello’s famous sketch “Who’s on First?” takes a typically hard line: She pretends not to get the joke so she can cast “herself as the neurodivergent entrepreneur who operated on a different wavelength,” as opposed to a scheming criminal of the tawdriest kind.

On the other side, you have what Carreyrou describes as “cinephiles’ lofty debates about truth and art.” These debates revolve around how we should feel about the obvious but bizarrely repressed fact that Holmes is totally captivating, the source of the film’s eerie power. She is both a loving mother and a cartoon character with her Looney Tunes eyes, possessed of a dreamy gaze that is common to saints and madwomen alike. When the tears slide across the plane of her face — which under Oppenheim’s zoom lens takes up the entire screen, the entire world — it is as if we can see something fracturing inside her, some horrible realization taking hold as she prepares for life in prison. For those who don’t share Carreyrou’s unforgiving take, this “glimpse into her soul” presents a problem: What if we’re being duped? What if we ourselves are exposed as sentimental fools? The result is a wary coolness flowing under the warm effusions of praise for the movie, as critics warn that “one’s empathy may easily be exploited.”

I say let the feelings flourish. You shouldn’t feel bad for feeling bad for Elizabeth Holmes. Not because maybe she is neurodivergent, or because she appears to be surrounded by men, including Fielder and Oppenheim, intent on using her for their own ends. Rather, because she represents something all too knowable and familiar.

This is not to say that, under the camera’s watchful gaze, Holmes transforms into an honest broker. Quite the contrary. In another instantly notorious scene, she tells Fielder that she has never told a lie — which is, of course, a lie. It is so bald-faced, so ludicrous, so unlikely to convince Fielder or anyone else, that you start to realize Holmes’s issues go beyond mere falsity, mere calculation, into the ruinous regions of self-deception, where she is struggling mightily to maintain some fiction of herself: namely, that she is not the sort of person who tells lies. She is not a liar, which is not something anyone wants to be. And here is where I find myself identifying with Holmes. I also believe that I am not a liar, even though I tell lies all the time. I probably lie every day. In a certain light, you could say that is in fact what I am, a liar.

I felt a similar pang of recognition in the scenes in which Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, attempt to resurrect Theranos, all hot-blooded purpose as they work the phones under the insane belief that they can relaunch a tarnished company whose founder is days away from entering prison. I am a writer after all. How many essays have been forged in the throes of manic inspiration, fired by the fantasies of tens of thousands (no, hundreds of thousands!) of readers, only to be met by the editor’s withering glare and the indifference of audiences? How could any of us do anything without a healthy dollop of self-deception to help us along the way?

The movie’s most poignant scene involves Fielder compelling Holmes to watch The Dropout, a televised dramatization of the Theranos scandal in which Holmes is played by Amanda Seyfried. As Seyfried gamely fangirls to Steve Jobs and shouts, “Get the fucking money!” and lets her former lover and Theranos partner Sunny Balwani fondle her, Holmes collapses in sobs and says she can no longer go on. Perhaps, as Carreyrou suggests, this is all for show, a plea for our mercy and affection. But let’s grant for a moment that her tears are genuine. Is Holmes upset because the television show is a true depiction, smashing the carapace of denial she has built around herself? Or is it rather that none of us could bear realizing what the world thinks we are like, which invariably is at odds with how we view ourselves?

Fielder and Oppenheim are not ones to open their thematic aperture too wide. As the documentary goes on, it becomes ever more narrowly focused on the question of whether Holmes is aware that Evans is trying to profit from the movie. But there are hints everywhere of a broader malaise emanating from Silicon Valley: Tesla Cybertrucks in a parking lot, a WeWork that Evans uses as his office space. These are (or were) companies run by men animated by delusions of grandeur, who like Holmes are not inclined to see themselves as bad people. Like everyone else, they have their reasons and excuses for their behavior. What I struggle to comprehend is a form of moral superiority that suggests we can’t possibly understand Elizabeth Holmes when we can — not only because her way of living is all around us, but because it’s inside us, too. That is what makes her tragic, if that is not too grandiose a word: a real-life Emma Bovary for the technological age.

For me, at any rate, that is why this odd bit of journalism (for that is what it is) is so moving, so transfixing. As the movie creeps toward its conclusion, there are surreal flashbacks of Fielder and Holmes swimming together in the frigid Pacific Ocean. At times they seem to be playing, frolicking almost; at others, she seems to be beseeching him, or he seems to be dragging her along. It is an image that can be interpreted in all kinds of ways: attraction and repulsion, forgiveness and betrayal, two creatures trapped in the same soup.
Your dreams may not foretell the future, but the way that your heart falls asleep just might.
Researchers have now shown that in the early stages of sleep, as the nervous system undergoes rapid changes, the heart's electrical activity can be used to determine future health risks.
All that is needed is the data from one electrocardiogram (ECG) lead, placed on the chest during sleep.
With that, artificial intelligence can predict someone's risk of an irregular heartbeat, stroke, heart failure, or death from any cause in the next 10 years.
The findings are published in the journal SLEEP, with support from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH).

"This new approach has the potential to identify individuals at risk for cardiovascular disease years before clinical symptoms arise," says David Goff, acting director of NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI).
"Evaluating whether this information improves traditional risk prediction is an important next step."
The research team, led by scientists at Emory University, first trained a deep learning system on the public health data of nearly 16,000 patients.
These patients were enrolled in a sleep study at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, and as part of the trial, they had their heart activity measured during sleep by an ECG.

Once trained, the AI system was then put to the test on two more datasets, including nearly 10,000 patients from Emory University Hospital and 13,000 patients from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston.
In the end, the model was able to sort participants into different levels of long-term cardiovascular risk.
After adjusting for conventional risk factors and sleep characteristics, the AI system could predict the 10-year risk of several cardiovascular outcomes.
For each standard deviation increase in the AI's risk score, there was a 103 to 172 percent higher risk of atrial fibrillation, which is an irregular heartbeat.
There was also a 19 to 40 percent higher risk of stroke, a 69 to 133 percent higher risk of heart failure, and a 65 to 82 percent higher risk of death from any cause.
Only one group showed a significantly increased risk of future myocardial infarction, or heart attack.

"Importantly, we found that adding the score from our deep learning model improved prediction of cardiac outcomes beyond established risk factors," says Gari Clifford, study author and professor of biomedical engineering at Georgia Institute of Technology.
"Adding these scores into sleep studies has great potential for improving early detection of cardiovascular disease, determining who is most at risk, and being more proactive in patient care."
Issues with sleep, like insomnia, are known risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
During a polysomnography (PSG) test, which is the gold standard for diagnosing sleep disorders, the heart is often recorded as well.
But unless this data throws up a serious red flag, the findings are rarely considered.
All that subtle information on cardiac function could be going to waste.
Traditional models for cardiovascular risk usually consider ECG recordings when a person is awake or walking.
But during sleep, they may also record important fluctuations.
Using a deep learning algorithm, researchers in the US have now found that ECG recordings show strong predictive value for cardiovascular health outcomes when combined with sleep stages.
That's true even when adjusting for other cardiovascular risk factors, such as age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and smoking.
During the lightest stage of sleep, for instance, changes to heart rate patterns and electrical conduction seem to be especially indicative of future health risks.
"These rapid autonomic fluctuations may amplify subtle abnormalities in heart-rate dynamics or conduction patterns," the authors explain.

In fact, incorporating ECG-derived data from sleep improved current cardiovascular risk models by up to 6 percent for atrial fibrillation, up to 9 percent for heart failure, and up to 7 percent for mortality prediction.
These absolute increases might seem modest, the authors explain, but they still improve our ability to separate individuals who do and do not develop heart failure beyond traditional means.
With continued development, the AI system has the potential to help health practitioners screen for patients with sleep disorders who may be at extra risk of heart failure.

"In the future, proven analytical approaches like this could be integrated into existing diagnostic tests for patients undergoing sleep studies as a screening tool for multiple adverse cardiovascular outcomes," says Goff.
The research has been published in SLEEP.
Roughly two of every five fighters in the Air Force fleet could be F-35As by 2035, according to a new fighter force structure report the service submitted to Congress on Oct. 16.

Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, revealed the new estimate during an Oct. 20 media roundtable at the Pentagon as he explained the report’s estimates of the future force’s mix of different types of fighters.
The Air Force did not provide a full copy of the report to reporters.

About 40 percent of the fleet could be F-35s, Tabor said. Another 20 percent would be a combination of F-22 Raptors and F-47s as the sixth-generation fighter replaces the Raptor. The Air Force built 186 operational F-22s, and Tabor said the Air Force still plans to replace them with roughly an equivalent number of F-47s. The remaining 40 percent of the fleet would likely be split evenly between F-15 Eagle variants and F-16 Fighting Falcons, Tabor said.
Source: Air Force figures cited by Tabor. Excludes A-10s. Percentages are approximate.
Currently, the fighter fleet—not counting A-10s—is split roughly 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s, and 10 percent F-22s.

Beyond the mix of the fighters, the force structure report also provides a new estimate of the total number of fighters the Air Force says it will need in the years to come: 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035.

That’s up from the 1,271 the service estimated it would have in 2026 and the 1,369 combat-coded fighters it was shooting for by 2030 in last year’s report, Tabor said. The additional 140 jets would be a mixture of F-35s, F-15EXs, and F-47s.

The data used for the previous report was “pretty old,” Tabor said, so the service’s researchers set out to compile fresher and more accurate information. This analysis was going on before combat operations against Iran broke out earlier this year, he said, and was not driven by the war.

The Air Force’s analysis was based on geographic combatant commanders’ reported requirements to achieve their goals at “medium risk,” Tabor said, and he cautioned that is based on their subjective assessments of what they will need—and will likely change in the future.

“Certainly, world events and changing requirements in the combatant commands will change that number,” Tabor said. “Capabilities that we bring on to platforms will change the number, and I think really importantly, technology will change the number.”

Getting to the new 2035 goal depends on two key factors falling into place, Tabor said. First, Congress will need to provide the funds the Air Force needs to buy the jets. And the defense industrial base—in particular, prime contractors Lockheed Martin and Boeing—must produce enough aircraft in time.

Top Air Force officials have for years said the service needs to buy 72 new fighters each year to replace its older, retiring jets and modernize the fleet. The fiscal 2027 budget request doesn’t reach that level, proposing 38 new F-35s and 24 F-15EXs for a total of 62. Tabor said those purchases can “ramp over time” to hit the numbers the Air Force needs.
“The question is, can industry produce at those levels?” Tabor said. “They’ve assured us that they can, and we believe them, but we also actually need to see it manifest.”

Right now, 2027’s funding levels remain a big question mark. The administration’s strategy for funding the Pentagon this year relies on a budget reconciliation bill to add additional funding priorities on top of the proposed “base” appropriations.

The Air Force’s proposed budget counted on $2.34 billion coming through reconciliation to pay for 14 of those 38 new F-35s. If reconciliation doesn’t pass, Tabor said, the Air Force is not out of options. It could try to find money in the base budget to pay for more F-35s, he said—though that would require pulling billions from other critical programs.
“We just lose 14 times [an] F-35’s worth of other capabilities that we were planning on,” Tabor said.
Or, he said, the purchases could be pushed out to 2028, which would further put the Air Force behind on reaching its fighter fleet goals.
“It is really imperative that we get the resourcing we need in order to modernize the Air Force the way we want it to be,” Tabor said. “We need it all.”
In the meantime, the clock is ticking on large portions of the Air Force’s fleet such as older F-15s and F-16s, which are aging and reaching the end of their lifespans.

The Air Force is considering buying a new version of the F-16, which is tentatively being referred to as the F-16G. But the Air Force has not yet made any decision on that, Tabor said, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.” That decision likely won’t be made as part of the 2028 budgeting process, he said, but perhaps the years that follow.

Older F-16s will reach the end of their lifespans in the mid-2030s, Tabor said, and “we are very conscious of that.” The simple—“and maybe the lazy”—way to approach that problem, Tabor said, is to automatically replace them with new F-16s. But that might not be the best strategy, he said.

“There is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” he said. “It’s not urgent, frankly. What we don’t want to get to is a point where it is urgent, and we haven’t done the homework and decided ‘hey, this is really the right place to be.’ We do have time to churn through that and make sure that we have a good option going forward.”

One advantage to buying more F-16s, which Lockheed Martin now builds in Greenville, S.C., is that “it’s practically a ready-made aircraft,” Tabor said—if the Air Force wants to stick with the same type of capabilities.

Another potential wrinkle is the Pentagon’s push to expand its multiyear procurement authorities. The Air Force is eyeing such agreements for the F-35 and F-15EX, though its request is pending before Congress. More multiyear procurement deals will help provide industry more financial stability, Tabor said, which could make it easier for them to expand and stabilize production of fighters.

But while the Air Force is rapidly preparing to add hundreds of autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft to its fleet—the goal is 500 airframes by 2032—Tabor said they’re not yet changing the service’s calculus on what fighter force it will need in the future.

“CCA is very much a reality,” Tabor said. “It is going to be a part of our future, and there is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters. That’s not the CCA that we have right now, but it is advancing very, very rapidly. We’re confident that it will play a major role in future versions of the fighter force structure report.”
Update Oct. 20, 7:06 p.m. EDT (2306 UTC): SpaceX scrubbed the launch, targets Wednesday afternoon.

SpaceX was set to launch a batch of 27 Starlink satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California Tuesday afternoon, but ran into what appears to have been a technical issue that wasn’t surmountable during their launch window.

Liftoff of the Falcon 9 rocket from the West Coast is now scheduled during a window that opens at 2:59 p.m. PDT (5:59 p.m. EDT / 2159 UTC) on Wednesday, Oct. 21. The rocket will fly on a southeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad.
SpaceX will launch the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number B1063. This will be its 36th flight and will become the second booster to reach three dozen flights.

Roughly 8.5 minutes after liftoff, B1063 will target a landing on the droneship, A Shortfall of Gravitas. If successful, this will be the 229th landing on this vessel and the 673rd Falcon booster landing to date.

During a third quarter earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, hours before the original launch time on Oct. 20, SpaceX Chief Operating Officer (COO) and President Gwynne Shotwell noted that the company added 1.6 million customers in that three-month period. She said the service was active across 174 markets globally.

In a filing to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), SpaceX noted that it closed the third quarter with more than 11,100 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, which includes the 26 Starlink Version 3 satellites launched during Starship Flight 14.

“The Starship launcher itself will provide additional capacity across markets and enable new sales in high-demand areas,” Shotwell said. “We expect the market for communications to grow far beyond just human communication that we traditionally think about. Connecting cars, robots, and the adoption of super intelligence (artificial intelligence) will increase communication demands not in percentages, but in orders of magnitudes.”
The SEC filing stated that connectivity revenue for the quarter was $5.2 billion, an increase of 22 percent from the previous quarter.

“Total costs and expenses for the Connectivity segment were up $974 million year-over-year, driven primarily by our growing satellite constellation, Starlink Kit deliveries, and marketing initiatives to support revenue growth,” SpaceX said in its filing.

Bret Johnsen, SpaceX Chief Financial Officer (CFO), said that the company’s ability to increase the flight rate of orbital Starship missions is critical for future revenue growth on the Starlink satellite internet side of their business.

“Looking ahead, the satellite roadmap is a key driver of both the capacity and capability of our connectivity segment,” Johnsen said. “Through the end of the year and throughout 2027, we expect to deploy [Starlink] V3 broadband satellites in meaningful volume, with each Starship launch ramping towards a payload that delivers over 20 times the downlink capacity of the current generation of Falcon 9 launches today.

“In parallel, we will ramp Starlink Mobile V2 satellites on Starship, starting in 2027, and leverage our newly enhanced wireless spectrum portfolio to expand our direct-to-device and become a major mobile carrier, as Gwynne mentioned, in the United States.”

SpaceX founder Elon Musk said the next Starship launch is anticipated in November and is planned to include a catch attempt of both the Ship and Super Heavy booster. The company is seeking approval for this from the Federal Aviation Administration.

A new study using a computer model developed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, along with the University of California, Irvine, and Dartmouth College, finds Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier could contribute more to sea level rise by the end of the century than some previous estimates. In some model simulations, the glacier’s contribution was as much as twice current projections.

While the glacier is a major contributor to global sea level rise, projecting its long-term impacts has proved challenging because of complex processes. The study, published Oct. 12 in Nature Communications, reduces that uncertainty by homing in on the transitional area where glacial ice is no longer bound to the land and, instead, is afloat.

Existing ice sheet models typically treat this transitional area as a distinct boundary, commonly labeled grounding lines. The researchers’ model instead, accounts for these areas as grounding zones — areas where seawater penetrates several miles beneath glacial grounded ice, lifting the ice during tidal cycles that can generate instabilities. The process introduces warmer seawater to the grounded ice, accelerating its melt and destabilizing the glacier more than a distinct line would allow.

Incorporating grounding zones improved the accuracy of the model’s ability to simulate glacial retreat. The model matched historical satellite data dating back to the 1990s four times more closely than models that don’t include this factor.
The researchers believe this model could provide more reliable information on glacier dynamics, informing coastal regions most impacted by higher sea levels.

Destined for Mars and beyond, NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will be humanity’s first fission-powered spacecraft to travel outside Earth’s orbit. Announced during NASA’s “Ignition” event, this mission will demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space, and progress is underway on its key element: the nuclear power module. To expedite development of the spacecraft, NASA and its partners have mutually agreed to key contract actions that will advance the SR‑1 Freedom mission.

“These contract actions not only reduce technical risk and help us maintain momentum toward our 2028 launch, but they also strengthen collaboration across our partners,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “These actions keep SR‑1 Freedom on track and ensure we’re building the strongest possible foundation for NASA’s first fission‑powered voyage beyond Earth orbit while developing technology extensible to a vibrant space nuclear future.”

Sierra Lobo Inc. will provide the nuclear power module’s closed Brayton cycle power conversion system, which converts thermal energy from its fission reactor into electrical power needed for SR-1 Freedom’s nuclear electric propulsion demonstration. The work will be conducted under the Space Flight Systems Development and Operations Contract III, awarded in 2024, to support spaceflight hardware design, development, testing, and operations at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

The power conversion system will be integrated with the fission reactor, which is being designed and developed by the Department of Energy (DOE)’s Idaho National Laboratory to complete the nuclear power module. NASA and DOE incorporate thorough safety standards throughout the design and development of the SR-1 Freedom spacecraft, including interagency safety reviews, continuous oversight by a NASA chief safety officer, regulatory compliance, and a rigorous safety design process focusing on hazards, failure tolerance, and nuclear safety. In addition, the nuclear reactor portion of SR-1 Freedom will remain inactive until the spacecraft leaves Earth orbit.

Launching in late 2028, SR‑1 Freedom will deliver the SkyFall science mission, a team of three Mars helicopters evolved from the Ingenuity design, to collect scientific data, demonstrate exploration zones, and identify potential water sources. The mission will pave the way for deep space exploration and next‑generation fission-powered systems designed to keep NASA’s Moon Base operating through periods of darkness and in locations where solar power alone is not sufficient.

‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.
Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.
If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.

On this view, the explanation for the epistemic force of intuition mirrors the explanation for the epistemic force of perception. Both states present certain facts as real (or present certain propositions as true) by virtue of a distinctive presentational phenomenology. Call this the phenomenal strategy. The difference between them lies simply in the character of this phenomenology. In perception, it is an empirical sensory experience of the external world; in intuition, it is an intellectual or conceptual experience that purportedly reveals the normative, modal or conceptual structure of the world. These are features of the world that we comprehend but can’t see – that gratuitous cruelty counts against taking an action (normative structure), that there could be no round square (modal structure), or that the lucky believer in fake-barn country still doesn’t really know (conceptual structure).
A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual

But this phenomenological theory of the epistemic significance of intuitions faces a serious difficulty, one pressed most forcefully by Timothy Williamson and Ernest Sosa. Many reflective people report that they do not experience anything like the intellectual phenomenology that quasi-perceptualism posits. For them, judging that a proposition ‘seems right’ involves no distinctive experiential quality at all. If intuition lacks the requisite phenomenology in these cases, then the quasi-perceptualist explanation of its epistemic force collapses. (It’s worth evaluating this in yourself: do you feel an experiential quality when evaluating the thought experiments?)

This is the so-called absent intuition challenge. The kind of robust, presentational phenomenology developed on the basis of quasi-perceptualism is something many people simply deny having. Consequently, either these individuals lack introspective access to their own intuitions (an uncharitable conclusion), or the epistemic force of intuition cannot depend on the presence of a special intellectual phenomenology. If intuitions are to justify in the way quasi-perceptualism claims, then something other than phenomenology must be doing the epistemic work.

This conclusion can be pushed further to call into question even the epistemic significance of phenomenology for perception. To see why, consider the phenomenon known as derealisation disorder. Individuals with this condition report that their perceptual experiences feel perfectly normal from the inside – the colours, shapes and sensory qualities are all intact – yet the world does not seem real to them. Their experiences lack any sense of disclosure or revelatory force. In this respect, derealisation is the mirror image of a perfect hallucination. In derealisation, the experience gets things right, but it doesn’t feel like anything is being revealed; in hallucination, the experience gets things wrong, yet it feels totally convincing. The implication is striking. Call this apparent disclosure of reality presentationality: a mental state is presentational when its content is apprehended as how things actually are, rather than merely as they are thought about or imagined. Derealisation shows that neither the information carried by a perceptual state nor the way that state feels are sufficient for presentationality. A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual. Phenomenology, then, cannot explain the epistemic force of perceptual seemings, let alone intuitions.

This suggests that defenders of quasi-perceptualism have been looking in the wrong place. Earlier, I noted that perceptual experience has two salient features: it has a rich phenomenology, and it seems to reveal the world to us. The phenomenal strategy seized on the first feature – understandably, given how vivid and conspicuous perceptual phenomenology is – and then treated it as the source of the second. But derealisation cases show that phenomenology can remain intact even when the experience loses its revelatory character. What matters for justification is not how we experience something, but how we apprehend it. On the view I defend, presentationality is a cognitive posture, a way of apprehending a content rather than a distinctive way the experience feels. And it is this posture, this way of grasping the world and not its phenomenological glow, that supplies perceptual experience with its epistemic force.

To see what this posture amounts to, it helps to contrast it with more widely discussed attitudes. Belief, for example, is assertive: it commits us to the truth of its content. Imagination, by contrast, is non-assertive: it entertains possibilities without treating them as actual. Presentational attitudes (that is, seemings) occupy a middle ground. This cognitive posture is what makes a seeming capable of justifying a belief: it presents reality without committing to it, offering us a direct but defeasible route to acceptance.

Once we understand presentationality in this way, the case of intuition falls naturally into place. A crucial feature of presentational states is that they are happenings, not actions. They occur in us; we do not perform them. So, when something intuitively seems true, we do not decide to have this intuition any more than we decide to see a tree. It arrives unbidden. This passivity is precisely what allows a seeming to present its content as actual. When an intuition strikes us, we are not making a judgment or forming a belief. We are apprehending the content as the way things are. The intuition presents the scenario as actual in a manner that calls for belief. In this respect, intuitive seemings share the same role as perceptual seemings.
Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure

Understood in this way, the absent-intuition challenge dissolves. The quasi-perceptualist assumed that intuition’s presentational force must arise from an intellectual phenomenology analogous to the sensory phenomenology of perception. But if presentationality is a cognitive posture rather than a phenomenological glow, then no special ‘intellectual experience’ is needed. A person may have no distinctive phenomenology when an intuition arises and yet still apprehend the content as actual in the relevant sense. And once a content is apprehended as actual, it is reasonable to form the corresponding belief. The quasi-perceptualist is right that intuition and perception share something fundamental, but wrong about what that shared feature is. It is not a proprietary phenomenology, but the nature of the apprehension itself.

Why should apprehending a content as actual have any epistemic significance? The answer, I think, is simple. Presentational states are the cognitive events that place us in contact with the world or, more precisely, that seem to place us in contact with the world. When something presents itself to us as being the case, our default cognitive response is to form the corresponding belief. When I turn the corner of a building and my eyes fall on a tree, the tree is simply there before me. Believing that there is a tree is not normally a conclusion I draw; rather I simply accept what my experience presents to me. This is not a matter of inference or deliberation; it is the natural way a rational mind responds to what it takes to be reality.

Belief-formation is less like drawing a conclusion and more like yielding to a disclosure. When the apprehension is accurate, this default response reliably produces true belief; when it is not, the response is still intelligible and reasonable. Presentational states are epistemically respectable because they are where the world shows up for us: the point at which reality makes its first claim on belief. Intuitions inherit this status. They are simply the presentational events through which we apprehend the conceptual structure of a situation as actual, and in doing so provide a rational basis for belief without the need for any further epistemic mechanism.

Intuition saturates our ordinary reasoning. Whenever we see what follows from something, notice that something counts in favour of some action, or recognise something as a possible course of action, we are relying on intuition. These moments rarely announce themselves. They do not arrive with phenomenological fanfare. They are woven into the background of our deliberation, operating quietly whenever we take in a situation and immediately apprehend its normative or conceptual contours.

In this sense, intuition is to cognition what perception is to our engagement with the physical world. Perception allows us to navigate our environment by revealing how things stand around us; intuition allows us to navigate the space of reasons, norms and possibilities by revealing how things stand within the conceptual landscape. When we deliberate, we constantly rely on intuitions to apprehend which considerations matter, how they bear on one another, and what follows from them. Intuition is the cognitive means by which the conceptual structure of a situation is revealed to us.

Seen in this light, the thought experiments with which we started no longer appear as philosophical curiosities. They are simply highly controlled instances of a capacity we rely on constantly. When we imagine a runaway trolley or a real barn surrounded by fakes, we are not invoking a mysterious faculty or peering into a metaphysical telescope. We are exercising the same basic capacity we use when we imagine telling a difficult truth to a friend or weigh up different possible courses of action. The only difference is that philosophical cases are crafted to isolate a specific conceptual relation. Their dramatic trappings obscure the fact that they depend on the same presentational attitude at work in more mundane reasoning.
Intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it

This brings thought experiments back down to earth. Their epistemic significance arises not from exotic subject matter or imaginary scenarios, but from the fact that they trigger intuitions that disclose how certain concepts hang together. To see what it means for concepts to ‘hang together’, consider a familiar principle of storytelling: show, don’t tell. When J R R Tolkien in The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) describes the creature Gollum leading Frodo into the spider Shelob’s lair, he needn’t pause to explain: ‘This is an act of betrayal.’ The narrator doesn’t mark the moment when Gollum’s loyalties shift, or when his intentions cross a moral threshold. We grasp it directly from the unfolding of events. The situation presents itself as a betrayal: the actions, motives and dangers align in a way that demands the application of the concept. That is what I mean when I say that intuitions reveal how concepts hang together. They disclose the otherwise unstated conceptual requirements of a situation.

Now, a sceptic might argue that what is doing the work here is not intuition, but simply our skill at applying concepts. On this view, we respond correctly to cases because we are good at classifying situations. But this misses something crucial about the rationality of these classifications. To apply a concept is to act; it is to make a classificatory judgment. And judgments of this sort are not self-justifying. Simply deciding, without any basis, that a character has betrayed a friend would be epistemically arbitrary. Such judgments must themselves be grounded in something. Intuitions occur in us prior to and independently of any judgment. When a scenario strikes us as a clear instance of betrayal, that intuitive seeming is not itself an act of concept application. It is the pre-judgmental apprehension that makes the resulting judgment (the resulting application of the concept of betrayal) reasonable. In this sense, intuition does not compete with concept application. It enables it.

This same phenomenon of intuitive apprehension preceding judgment also shows up in ordinary perception. When we open our eyes, the world does not appear as a mosaic of colours and shapes. It appears as a scene populated with meaningful objects: a child reaching for a toy, a cat waiting expectantly for dinner, a car approaching too fast. As P F Strawson observed, if we try to describe what we see using only low-level sensory terms (patches of colour, shifting brightness), we falsify the experience. The world comes to us in perception already organised by concepts. What is presented is not bare visual data but things of certain kinds, situated in relations to one another.

And here, intuition enters even into everyday perceptual experience itself. Perception reveals not merely visual arrays but robust, three-dimensional situations that are concept-laden. This becomes particularly vivid in cases where expertise comes into play. Imagine walking through a field with a trained herpetologist. You both see a snake. Your sensory experience may be phenomenologically indistinguishable from hers – the same curves of the body, the same mottled pattern. Yet what is presented to each of you differs. To you, it is simply a snake. To her, it is an Agkistrodon contortrix. The difference is not in your visual apparatus per se but in the concepts at work within perception. Her grasp of the relevant distinctions generates a conceptually richer, even if phenomenologically identical, presentational state. And because intuitions are not phenomenologically robust, there is no need for any difference in how things look. This is why perceptual expertise can subtly transform experience without altering its sensory character.

Perception, then, is a perfect illustration of the broader point about intuitions. Because they lack any robust phenomenology, intuitions serve their function in plain view without our taking explicit notice of them.

The person who declines to get in the stranger’s car, or who flags the email as a phishing attempt, or who walks away from the deal – these individuals are not acting irrationally or on mere feeling. They are responding to a genuine presentational state: something is showing up as creepy, fraudulent or wrong. The situation is presenting itself as having a certain character, and that presentation carries epistemic weight – not because it is infallible, but because it is the same kind of state that grounds all of our most basic cognitive contact with the world.

This is precisely what philosophers mean when they talk about intuition. The difference between the person on the bridge who immediately senses that pushing the bystander is wrong, and the person who declines to get into a stranger’s car, is not a difference in kind. It is a difference in context and control. The philosopher’s thought experiment is a deliberately engineered situation designed to isolate and interrogate a single intuitive response. The everyday case is messier, embedded in a richer context, and rarely examined. But the underlying capacity, the presentational apprehension of how things are, is the same.

What has been missing in our theorising, until now, is simply the explicit recognition of this continuity. Philosophers have a well-developed account of why rational intuitions carry epistemic weight. They have been slower to claim that this account extends naturally to the intuitions we act on every day. Once we see this, ‘vibes’ and gut feelings are neither vindicated wholesale nor dismissed as mere noise. Instead, they are brought into the same framework that governs our most careful reasoning. The task of philosophy, then, is not to decide whether to trust intuition. It is to understand the role it already plays, from the thought experiment to the uneasy feeling about a stranger, in almost every act of understanding.

More than five years after revealing that she had multiple sclerosis (MS), Christina Applegate announced on Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with the condition on the most recent episode of her and Jamie Lynn Sigler’s podcast, MeSsy. This was her first time back on the show, she said, after taking a seven-month break to “process” the news after receiving it from her doctor.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’” Applegate recalled on the podcast. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.” Now, she says she’s “back at square one,” working with doctors to try to identify the actual cause of her debilitating symptoms.

As it turns out, what happened to Applegate isn’t all that unusual. According to a 2019 study out of Cedars-Sinai, nearly 20 percent of patients once informed they were suffering from MS were actually given the wrong diagnosis.

But why is a condition estimated to affect nearly one million people in the United States misdiagnosed so frequently? And why are these misdiagnoses so problematic? Rolling Stone spoke with a neurologist specializing in MS to find out.

Multiple sclerosis is a chronic, progressive neurological disorder as well as an immune-mediated disease, meaning it causes an abnormal immune system response. (Autoimmune diseases, when the body attacks its own healthy tissue, are a subset of immune-mediated disease.) More specifically, in MS, the immune system damages myelin, the protective coating around the nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. Myelin’s job is to help nerves send messages quickly, so when it’s compromised, messages between your brain and body slow down or get blocked altogether, causing MS symptoms.

The symptoms of MS can vary from person to person, as well as during the course of the disease, depending on which nerve fibers are affected. Common symptoms include numbness or tingling of the face, torso, or limbs; extreme mental and/or physical fatigue; vision problems (like double vision or inflammation of the optic nerve); muscle weakness; and dizziness. In some cases, MS can cause mood and/or cognitive changes.

However, in some cases, people who go on to be diagnosed with MS don’t have any symptoms. “It’s called radiologic isolated syndrome,” says Tirisham Gyang, MD, a neurologist and associate professor of neurology at the Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. “They get an MRI for a different reason, like headaches or an accident. Nobody is thinking they have MS. They’ve never had any symptoms of MS. Yet the brain MRI looks just like MS.”
Because of the evolving understanding of multiple sclerosis, the diagnostic criteria were revised in 2024 to be more sensitive and specific.

Prior to that, MS was exclusively a clinical diagnosis — meaning the patient had to have specific symptoms, like vision loss or weakness, for example. In addition to this, they would need to have results consistent with MS from tests like an MRI or spinal tap, Gyang says.

“It’s like a puzzle we’re trying to build,” she tells Rolling Stone. “We’re putting pieces together — the clinical aspect, the MRI, the spinal fluid, the vision test — and we try to figure out if they fit the criteria for MS.”
The revised diagnostic criteria includes additional tests that are more likely to lead to an accurate diagnosis. Applegate was diagnosed with MS in 2021, before these new benchmarks were established.
Why is multiple sclerosis misdiagnosed so frequently?

While at least two studies found that roughly 20 percent of MS patients were misdiagnosed, other research puts that number even higher. A 2019 study published in the journal Neurology indicated that “of all new referrals to MS subspecialty centers with a question of MS diagnosis, 30%–67% were ultimately determined not to have MS.”
Women, like Applegate, are at an even greater disadvantage. A 2021 study out of Argentina found that women were 83 percent more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than men.
A major reason for all the misdiagnoses is the lack of a definitive diagnostic biomarker of MS. “There’s no magic blood test that I’m aware of that is exclusively going to diagnose MS,” Gyang says.

Additionally, MS shares both symptoms and MRI findings with other diseases, complicating diagnoses. For example, MS can look a lot like migraine, vascular disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes, among other conditions, which can make definitive diagnoses more difficult, according to Gyang.

Misdiagnosis also may occur when the clinicians don’t apply the diagnostic criteria correctly, or rush through the process. “You don’t get a trophy for saying on the first day you see a patient that they have MS,” Gyang says. “Sometimes the additional piece of the puzzle we need is time. MS is not a static disease; it evolves over time.” In cases when a patient falls into a diagnostic gray area — where it’s unclear whether or not they have MS — she typically suggests that they repeat the tests in six months to see what, if anything, has changed.

To start with, it often means that patients are taking risky and unnecessary drugs. “These are immune suppressive or immune modulating treatments,” Gyang explains. “A patient without MS should not be on medication like that.”

Being treated for MS is also extremely expensive. “And it’s not just the treatments,” Gyang says. “It’s the blood work you have to get to monitor you while you’re on the treatment, [and] the time off you have to take from work to go for infusions. MS is a huge commitment and a huge burden.”
Another factor is that if someone has been misdiagnosed with MS and actually has a different condition, it means that their real diagnosis — and proper treatment — has been delayed, Gyang explains.

And then there’s the psychological impact of an MS misdiagnosis. “It’s traumatizing to patients to all of a sudden pull their diagnosis because some people have made peace with it, [or] have formed community,” Gyang says. “It’s very difficult having that discussion and saying ‘This is not MS. You have to start from square one.’ Sometimes that’s more frustrating to patients, and they would rather have a serious chronic disease because they have accepted that diagnosis.”

Ultimately, Gyang says that Applegate coming forward about her misdiagnosis will help bring awareness of the challenges of MS. “I know it’s intimidating and it’s scary, and it’s difficult to navigate the health system,” she says. “But we want patients to be empowered, and if there’s nobody that’s advocating for them, to find a voice to advocate for themselves.”

Kurosawa Kiyoshi and “Ju-on” director Shimizu Takashi are among the seven filmmakers behind “Night Tales Club,” a six-part Japanese supernatural anthology series set to premiere on Disney+ and Hulu in January 2027.

Yamada Takayuki leads the series as Hojo, a high-flying businessman fixated on the unexplained who acts as its storyteller. Each episode adapts a different tale from author Sawamura Ichi’s collection of short horror stories. Sawamura also adapted the material for the screen.

Hojo is convinced that ghosts, curses and other paranormal events are “bugs” – glitches that point to a hidden conspiracy. To get to the bottom of it, he offers JPY20 million ($126,000) in gold to anyone willing to come to his gathering, the Night Tales Club, and present a firsthand account of the supernatural along with proof. Six such accounts make up the series as Hojo chases the truth behind them.

Kurosawa, whose credits include “Cure” and “Wife of a Spy,” and Shimizu, known for “Ju-on” and “The Inugami Family,” each take one episode. So do Katayama Shinzo (“Gannibal,” “The Human Vapor”), Sode Yukiko (“Aristocrats,” “All the Lovers in the Night”), Sakashita Yuichiro (“I Can’t Cry With Your Face,” “Blonde”) and Nakamura Yosuke (“Higuma!!,” “Poison Girl”). Nakajima Kenji (“The Naked Director,” “Tokyo Swindlers”) directs the Hojo sequences.
Wakabayashi Yusuke and Yamamoto Teruhisa produce.
“As the original author of these stories, I feel an enormous sense of surprise and joy that they will soon be available on screen to scare audiences around the world.” Sawamura said.

The show joins a growing lineup of Japanese series on the streamer. Disney+ already carries “Gannibal,” in which a police officer stumbles on something sinister in a remote village, and “Land of Tanabata,” about a college student with an apparently pointless power who looks into a murder. Lighter fare includes cross-cultural romantic comedy “Merry Berry Love” and comedy variety show “The One Shot.”

Two extraordinarily rare fossils found in Wyoming have revealed a strange new species of squid relative that lived approximately 160 million years ago, during the Jurassic Period.

Named Wyoteuthis linsterorum, the prehistoric creature belonged to an extinct group of marine animals known as belemnites, which were related to modern squid and octopuses. What makes this species particularly remarkable is its unusually thick, barrel-shaped internal skeleton, earning it the distinction of being the "chunkiest" or "fattest" belemnite ever identified.

An international research team from the United States, United Kingdom, and New Zealand, including Dr. Dean Lomax, an Honorary Research Fellow at The University of Manchester, detailed the discovery in the scientific journal Papers in Palaeontology.
An Unusually Thick Jurassic Squid Relative

Belemnites are among the most frequently discovered fossils in the world. They are best known for their distinctive, bullet-shaped internal skeletal structures, called rostra or guards, which are often the only parts of the animals that survive in the fossil record.

Wyoming's Sundance Formation, which preserves evidence of an ancient inland sea that once stretched across much of the western United States, has yielded millions of these fossils. According to Wyoming paleontologist and study coauthor Jessica Lippincott, they are commonly nicknamed "squid butts" in the region.

Most belemnite fossils from Wyoming have a narrow, bullet-shaped appearance, typically measuring between 5 and 10 centimeters in length and just 1 to 2 centimeters across. The newly identified species is dramatically different. Its rostrum measures approximately 10 centimeters long but reaches an extraordinary 6 centimeters in width, making it the thickest known example of its kind.
Scientists estimate that the living animal, including its arms, could have reached a total length of approximately 60 centimeters, or about two feet.
Rare Fossils Reveal a Surprising Evolutionary Secret

Wyoming paleontologist Bill Wahl, who has devoted much of his career to searching for fossils across the state, recognized that the unusual specimen deserved closer examination. He said the belemnite "stuck out like a sore thumb" compared with the countless others found in the region.

Wahl assembled an international team to investigate the fossils, bringing in specialists including belemnite expert Alexey Ippolitov, a PhD student now based at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand.

The researchers used computed tomography (CT) scanning to investigate the fossils' internal structures without damaging the specimens. These detailed scans revealed an unexpected connection to an ancient belemnite family that scientists had believed disappeared millions of years before this animal lived.

Ippolitov said he was "deeply surprised" to encounter such an unusual specimen from a group that has already been studied extensively. Belemnites have been the subject of paleontological research for more than 200 years, making the identification of such a radically different species especially remarkable.
The creature's unusual proportions may also offer clues about how it lived and hunted.

Ippolitov explains: "A possible explanation is that their relatively large size gave them an advantage when hunting co-occurring smaller belemnites of the genus Pachyteuthis. Modern squid, after all, are hardly picky when it comes to prey: they readily hunt not only other species of cephalopods, but sometimes even their own kind."
A Fossil Discovery Nearly 30 Years in the Making
Although the species has only now been formally described, its discovery began almost three decades ago.

The first known specimen was found in the late 1990s by Dr. Burkhard Pohl, founder of the Wyoming Dinosaur Center. While examining fossils, Pohl noticed a belemnite that was considerably larger than any he had previously encountered.
Despite its unusual appearance, the specimen remained unstudied in a museum collection drawer for many years.

A breakthrough came when fossil collector Cliff Linster discovered a second specimen near Ten Sleep, Wyoming. He donated the fossil to the Wyoming Dinosaur Center in 2019, providing researchers with another example of the mysterious animal.
With two specimens available for comparison, scientists finally had enough evidence to recognize and formally describe an entirely new species.

The genus name Wyoteuthis means "a squid from Wyoming," while the species name linsterorum recognizes Cliff Linster and his family for their contributions. Linster discovered one of the only two known examples and ensured it was available for scientific research.
Lippincott emphasized how extraordinary the discovery was, even for researchers familiar with Wyoming's abundant belemnite fossils.

"After spending years fossil hunting in Wyoming and collecting countless fossils of the common Pachyteuthis belemnites here in Wyoming, this one is unlike anything I have ever seen! It goes to show that we are still finding new species of fossils all the time, and people who rockhound or collect invertebrate fossils can also contribute to science."
Honoring a Fossil Hunter's Remarkable Legacy

Sadly, Cliff Linster passed away in June before the research was published. He had been aware that scientists were investigating his discovery and was enthusiastic about seeing the unusual fossil receive formal scientific recognition.
The Linster family already had an impressive history of fossil discoveries, including their association with the famous dinosaur Bambiraptor.

For British paleontologist Dr. Dean Lomax, the discovery also carries considerable personal meaning. Lomax, an Honorary Research Fellow at The University of Manchester and an 1851 Research Fellow at the University of Bristol, first worked alongside Cliff and his wife, Sandy, while excavating dinosaur fossils as a teenager.

He said: "I met Cliff and Sandy in 2009, when I spent a week digging up a dinosaur bonebed on their property in northern Montana. I have fond memories of that dig, listening to Cliff share his passion for fossils, including this belemnite. I'm honored to help name this fossil after Cliff. It's bittersweet that he didn't get to see it published, but it's wonderful that we can immortalize him and his family name in the history of paleontology. The find is incredibly rare, which might be due to some ecological adaptations to the environment at the time. Perhaps its rarity is a result of narrow specialization."

Lomax has extensive experience studying Wyoming's prehistoric animals, including collecting fossils and excavating plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs from the Sundance Formation. He is also the author of the recently published book "The Secret Lives of Dinosaurs," which features fossils from Wyoming.
The discovery highlights how even well-studied fossil groups can still hold major surprises, particularly when unusual specimens are preserved and made available for scientific investigation.

Both known fossils of Wyoteuthis linsterorum are now on display at the Wyoming Dinosaur Center in Thermopolis, Wyoming, where visitors can see the extraordinary remains of one of the Jurassic seas' most unusual squid relatives.
The findings are published in the international journal Papers in Palaeontology.
