COP17: The world has a plan to save nature. Is it working?

The UN Secretary-General has called for an end to the “war on nature”. On Monday, governments gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, will have to confront a more practical question: are they doing enough to win the peace and put the world’s biodiversity goals back on track?

COP17, the UN Biodiversity Conference, comes at a critical halfway point in the global effort to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. Running from 19 to 30 October, the meeting will take stock of progress, identify where countries are falling behind and, crucially, consider how to accelerate action over the next four years.
First things first: What is the global biodiversity framework?
The big picture: Think of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as the world’s blueprint for halting and reversing the destruction of nature.

Agreed in 2022, it contains 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals for 2050. It tackles the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
Its best known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

But, the framework goes much further, including financing for biodiversity, reforming harmful incentives, encouraging more sustainable production and consumption and addressing businesses’ impacts and dependencies on nature.
Reality check: We’re not moving fast enough.

There has been movement. Nearly 90 per cent of the 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 per cent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans and more than 70 per cent have submitted national reports.

But, fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties are on track. Ambition also remains short of the 30-by-30 goal, while major gaps persist in finance, capacity, cooperation and the data needed to track progress.
As Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders in Yerevan on Friday: “Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability.”
Why it matters: COP17 is essentially about moving from promises to delivery.
Among the big issues governments will grapple with:
- Taking stock: Countries will undertake the first global review of collective progress under the framework, examining what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed.
- Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.

- Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030, including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Paruyr Hovhannisyan.

- Making the Cali Fund work: Governments will have an opportunity to advance practical arrangements for the fund, designed to support fair and equitable benefit-sharing from commercial use of digital sequence information on genetic resources.
- Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results.
- Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.
For host Armenia, success means COP17 becoming both a “review COP” and an “implementation COP”.
“We cannot treat 2030 as a distant deadline,” Ambassador Hovhannisyan told UN News. “Decisions taken in Yerevan must help close the gap between commitments and results on the ground.”

Hambardzum Matevosyan, Armenia’s Environment Minister and incoming COP17 president, puts the progression simply: COP15 produced the framework and COP16 advanced mechanisms to implement it. COP17, he said, must establish “where we stand, what is working, where progress is falling short and what must change”.
Biodiversity can sound abstract. Its loss is anything but.

As António Guterres reminded leaders on Friday, the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe depend on it. The question in Yerevan is whether countries can turn an ambitious global agreement into action quickly enough.

On Thursday, launching a major UN report evaluating global progress under the landmark Kunming framework, Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, distilled the challenge: “We know where we stand. We know where the gaps are. Now, we must work together to close them.”

There is a before and after watching The Devils in my life, and I suspect many of its admirers feel the same way. You rarely see the Warner Bros. logo in the credits of a big-budget film in which a nun masturbates with a charred femur, but such was director Ken Russell’s vision of a real case of religious and political hysteria in 1634 France. Would you believe it was so widely condemned that it’s been virtually impossible to watch in full since its 1971 release? In what might be Warner’s only good decision this year, the studio is atoning for its censorship sins by releasing a 4K restoration of the director’s original cut across cinemas.

The Devils is Russell’s masterpiece, but the rest of his wildly prolific filmography is not far behind. The man had style down, unafraid to go full-tilt into camp fantasia while always staying grounded in fierce intellect. Ever the proper English schoolboy, many of his works are biographies of composers and literary figures, only the subjects are framed as sex-crazed, prog-rock addicts who confer with a Judy Garland–stanning pope and befriend divalicious female leads. (Russell was, against all odds, straight.) Here are 11 films to get into once you’ve walked off The Devils’s daze can fully surrender to Russellmania. All of his films are singular: You might abhor one and adore another, but each will pull you to the next.

Russell’s first major hit is the epitome of still waters running deep. Based on the D.H. Lawrence novel (this is also a reading list!), it masquerades as a quiet romantic drama about two sisters before turning into a carnal merry-go-round with their men, the impossibly sexy Alan Bates and Oliver Reed, who get naked and wrestle for the fun of it. Larry Kramer nabbed an Oscar nomination for his screenplay here, long before his legendary activism, and Glenda Jackson took home the Best Actress trophy — before also blazing a career fearless in politics and artistry. ➽ Available through the Criterion Collection.

No one captures mania like Russell, and what is passion for music if not a passion for the mania that drives our basest impulses? The Music Lovers is a dual portrait of the off-kilter relationship between the gay composer Tchaikovsky and his hypersexual wife, Nina. Using much of the legendary Russian’s symphonies and structured, almost wordlessly, as one large movement, it finds their true devotion to each other in their love of music. ➽ Streaming on MGM+.

Russell’s love letter to classic Hollywood is dizzying in its relentless motion, almost a sugar headache, but never less than glorious to behold. This meta-adaptation of the 1953 musical, already an irreverent take on the century’s earlier stage spectacles, was another early hit for the director. Russell adds a 30 Rock–esque backstage frame in which an assistant stage manager (Twiggy, looking divine) is thrust into the spotlight when the star of her regional playhouse’s production of The Boy Friend is nowhere to be found. ➽ Streaming on Apple TV.

Maybe my favorite Russell, after The Devils, is this dual study of the little-remembered French sculptor Henri Gaudier and the even more obscure writer Sophie Brzeska. Both lived what some might romanticize as chic, Parisian bohemia (perennially broke and largely unrecognized within their lifetimes), and both experienced what we would now diagnose as severe mental illness. Russell doesn’t traffick in any of that, and screenwriter Christopher Logue refuses to pathologize the two, focusing instead on the untamed beauty of their relationship, which was romantic, familiar, treacherous, and pure. It’s one of Russell’s quieter films, allowing his fervor to flow directly from his subjects, but he pairs it with stunning, art-book-worthy depictions of Gaudier’s works. Its final shot, in which Brzeska accepts her role as the keeper of her companion’s legacy, an image that acknowledges the inseparability of their art and life, is breathtaking. ➽ Streaming on Apple TV.

Probably the best-known of Russell’s works is his adaptation of the Who’s Tommy, fronted by the band’s Roger Daltrey, with cameos by Tina Turner, Elton John, and Jack Nicholson. It also has surely the most un-Oscar-bait-y performance ever to score a nomination, from poor Ann-Margret, who was made to writhe around in Champagne and baked beans. And guess what? I hate it; an instance of the director going overboard with his frenetic style. The Broadway version is my favorite take on the rock opera, since it streamlines so much of the story’s raggediness and woe-is-me boomerism. But you always have to hand it to the man for doing things his way. If reading this makes you think I’m an absolute square, congratulations! You will love this movie, and we can toast at the next Russell convention. ➽ Streaming on Apple TV.

If you didn’t immediately look into the aforementioned Judy Garland reference, you’ll find it in Russell’s second collaboration with Roger Daltrey — in the same year, the workaholic — which is also his most out-there biopic. As with The Music Lovers, it takes off from the lesser-known account of an established genius’s lover, framing the 19th-century composer Franz Liszt as a clueless sex addict who is nevertheless angelic compared to the fascistic Wagner, later portrayed as an evil Superman (logo and all!) who commands a pre–Star Wars imperial army. In his recent review, film critic Brandon David Wilson wrote that “so many of you think you’ve seen a totally liberated film but you haven’t.” Does that make it a good film? Not really, but it’s Russell at his most orgiastic. ➽ Streaming on Apple TV.

In this surreal voyage into consciousness, one of Russell’s better-known studio releases, a researcher starts experimenting with hallucinogenics and sensory-deprivation tanks, sending him (and the film) into some of the director’s trippiest visuals. What’s crazy is that it begins almost like a scene cut from Indiana Jones — all classrooms and academia — before turning into a creature feature and eventually, basically, Russell’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. ➽ Streaming on Tubi.

The list’s shortest pitch: Kathleen Turner as a sex worker named China Blue being chased around by Anthony Perkins, who plays a street preacher with an addiction to poppers and peep shows. ➽ Streaming on Tubi.

Russell never met an AP Lit story he couldn’t corrupt (or find the truth in?), and this one is no exception: a wildly sexual, opium-fueled retelling of that fateful night when Mary Shelley (Natasha Richardson in her film debut) dreamed up the Frankenstein myth to win a writing competition against her incestuous, literary circle, which included husband Percy and Lord Byron. The extreme hedonism of it all might … not … actually … be far from the truth. ➽ Streaming on Tubi.

This one’s earned cult-favorite status in recent years, thanks to people online discovering how yummy Hugh Grant’s hair looks in it and the fact that its plot, based on a Bram Stoker novel, is basically the same as SpongeBob SquarePants’s Alaskan Bull Worm episode. For fans of Hellraiser and its era of twisted English fairy tales with harrowing practical effects, White Worm wakes up a sleepy rural town with the accidental digging up of an ancient serpent’s skull (oops!), which sets off a chain of murders orchestrated by a slinky lady of the manor who is secretly a dark priestess. Those without Halloween costumes: Turn to Amanda Donohoe. Russell was losing prestige and funding by this point in his career, resulting in some truly zany sequences shot on video that, while thematically similar, make the 35-mm.-shot Devils look like stained glass. It’s gnarly and fun as hell, though. ➽ Streaming on Tubi.

If you’ve made it this far through the list, you probably own a caftan, or at least have an old-school queen in your life whom you simply adore. Treat them to this silly little romp, which sees all-time queen Oscar Wilde and his lover taking in a secret performance of the writer’s Salome at a friend’s brothel. The most overtly queer of Russell’s works, it sneaks in some touching and venomous commentary on censorship and life on the margins. It’s the type of left-field passion project that makes you love an artist, and Imogen Millais-Scott’s titular performance is one for the ages — especially considering she’d gone blind three weeks before shooting. ➽ Streaming on Tubi.
Senior enlisted leaders aboard submarines will now fall under the rating of Chiefs of the Boat, replacing a billet-based designation with a formal rating for the role.

A U.S. Navy administrative message, or NAVADMIN, released Monday, establishes the Submarine Chief of the Boat as a general rating equivalent to a command master chief. The Navy said the change is intended to provide a clearer career path, specialized training and advancement opportunities for submarine sailors seeking the leadership position.

The Chief of the Boat, or COB, serves as the commanding officer’s principal enlisted adviser, responsible for issues affecting sailors’ welfare, morale, job satisfaction and utilization, according to the Navy’s enlisted occupational standards.

Previously, the COB was assigned by billet and identified by Navy Enlisted Classification 8COB, according to the Navy’s personnel manual. The existing policy specified a normal 36-month tour and allowed submarine sailors in paygrades E-8, E-8 selectee and E-9 to qualify for the designation.

Under the previous policy, selection involved a screening process for sailors seeking the assignment. Those historical requirements should not be assumed to remain in effect under the new rating; the NAVADMIN directs applicants to the submarine force’s senior enlisted program assignment instruction, COMSUBLANT/COMSUBPACINST 1306.2, for current application requirements and selection criteria.

The new rating is open to active-duty, submarine-designated sailors, all of whom must be submarine warfare qualified. Non-nuclear submarine ratings will be the primary source of candidates, though other submarine-designated personnel may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Selected Reserve sailors are not eligible.
The Navy will immediately convert E-9 personnel currently holding the 8COB designation to COBCM, according to the NAVADMIN.
The announcement does not specify how many sailors are expected to enter the new rating or detail how all existing selection and assignment procedures will change.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appointed Medal of Honor recipient and U.S. Marine Corps reservist Dakota Meyer to the Pentagon’s Barracks Task Force.

Meyer will now serve as Hegseth’s senior advisor to the task force, which is tasked with addressing the military’s “unacceptable” living conditions, the defense secretary announced Monday in a video on social media.

“Our warfighters should be focused on training, readiness and defending this great nation,” Meyer said during the video. “They shouldn’t have to fight for basic living conditions when they come home at night.”
As senior advisor, Meyer will travel to installations across the country, looking at their barracks, meeting with service members and identifying how to curtail any issues blocking the resolutions.

The first group of installations Meyer is expected to visit are all located in California, with Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton on Tuesday and Wednesday, followed by Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms on Thursday and Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on Friday.
If sticking to schedule, Meyer will have visited 21 bases across the country, with most along the East Coast, by the end of December, according to a map displayed during the social media video.

“I want you to ask this question for the next couple of months: Where’s Dakota?” Hegseth posed during the video. “Could he be coming to my base, to my installation, to my camp, my fort? Because he might be.”

“He’ll be traversing the country on behalf of the Barracks Task Force, on behalf of me personally inspecting, holding town halls, getting real input, and then providing real solutions,” Hegseth continued. “Be on the lookout for him.”

Hegseth first formed the task force in October 2025 to be led by the assistant secretary of defense for energy, installations and environment. The group is meant to identify investment opportunities and create department-wide policies for barracks standards.

The One Bill Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed into law in July 2025, gave the Defense Department $1.2 billion for barracks improvement, with $230 million allotted for the Marine Corps Barracks 2030 initiative and $425 million for enlisted boot camp barracks and other related facilities, as well as $1 billion for Army, Navy, Air Force and Space Force restoration and modernization of military housing.

A Government Accountability Office report from August found that the Defense Department does not request enough funding to meet its installation maintenance and improvement needs, resulting in an estimated $285 billion of maintenance backlogs in fiscal 2025.

Previous GAO reports found that some barracks were “chronically neglected,” resulting in poor conditions that impacted enlisted service members’ quality of life. Thousands of service members lived in subpar barracks, with some having potentially serious health and safety risks, according to a 2023 report.

Recently, the Barracks Task Force funded various projects at installations across the nation, including modernized housing at Fort Stewart-Hunter Army Airfield, Georgia, and a housing installation at Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton, Washington.
“From this point forward, there’s no confusion about who’s accountable,” Meyer posted on social media. “If we don’t get this fixed, there’s only one person to blame. Me.”

Former President Barack Obama awarded Meyer his Medal of Honor in 2011 for his service during the Battle of Ganjgal in Afghanistan in 2009 when he repeatedly entered an enemy ambush zone to rescue wounded comrades and recover the bodies of fallen service members. His actions were credited with saving 13 Americans and 23 Afghan personnel.
Meyer left the Marine Corps in 2010 and reenlisted in the reserves in April 2025, with his oath of enlistment administered at the Pentagon by Hegseth.

Ohio State may be without star quarterback Julian Sayin for the remainder of the season in what could be a significant blow to its national championship hopes.

Ohio State coach Ryan Day said Tuesday that Sayin would be out "indefinitely" and that may include the remainder of the season. No. 3 Ohio State will give both Luke Fahey and Tavien St. Clair first-team snaps this week during the bye week ahead of its next game against No. 16 USC on Oct. 31.

"Based on the nature of the injury we are putting together a plan for him not being available for the regular season and him also not being available for the postseason," Day said. "If he's not able to return this fall, we're putting together a plan for that, as well."

Sayin suffered an arm injury in the fourth quarter of the Buckeyes' 19-15 win over Indiana on Saturday. If Sayin is out for the remainder of the regular season, he would miss games against No. 16 USC, Oregon, Northwestern, Nebraska and Michigan. Before the injury, Sayin ranked third nationally in passing yards (2,007) and touchdowns (19).
The undefeated Buckeyes are in prime position to make the College Football Playoff – they are the No. 2 seed in – but the selection committee will take into account the impact of no Sayin.

Within the CFP protocol is the consideration of "the unavailability of key players and coaches that may have affected a team's performance during the season or likely will affect its postseason performance."
If Ohio State's play suffers without Sayin, that can have an impact.
If Sayin is indeed out for the season, that can have an impact.

If Sayin's progress improves and he is able to return this season – a seemingly unlikely proposition given Day's comments on Tuesday – Ohio State would likely get the benefit of the doubt if it lost a game that Fahey or St. Clair started against USC or Oregon. Conversely, that loss would take on even greater meaning if Fahey was expected to be the starter through the remainder of the season.

Consider it this way: It would almost be as if the selection committee was evaluating different teams. There's the Ohio State with Sayin and the Ohio State without Sayin. If the latter looks noticeably worse than the former, it could have a significant impact.

It is a situation that bears watching if Ohio State stays the course as a top playoff contender. If the Florida State playoff situation with Jordan Travis in 2023 has taught us anything, it is that a top team can be penalized if it is missing a key part of its offense. The undefeated Seminoles famously missed the four-team playoff in 2023 after Travis suffered a season-ending injury that the committee determined impacted FSU's outlook. If Ohio State doesn't look the same without Sayin, there is a precedent already for the Buckeyes to be penalized.

There's a lot still to like about Ohio State, from Heisman Trophy frontrunner Jeremiah Smith to one of the nation's top defenses that is holding opponents to 13.4 points per game. But how the selection committee views Ohio State without Sayin is now the most interesting College Football Playoff subplot as the calendar turns to the back half of the season.
